section_summary: This section documents political and diplomatic developments in Japan between October 1940 and January 1941, focusing on the consolidation of the domestic 'New Structure' and the formation of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association under Premier Fumimaro Konoe. It features extensive reporting and internal State Department analyses on military pressure on the Cabinet, Cabinet reorganizations including the appointment of Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma, and the constitutional friction surrounding the forthcoming session of the Imperial Diet. In addition, the section contains significant assessments of Japanese political sentiment, including an analysis of conservative commercial opinion in western Japan by Consul Walter P. McConaughy and a detailed proposal and memorandum by American businessman M. Kleiman advocating a special emissary to pursue U.S.-Japanese reconciliation.

subfiles.about: Reports on Japanese press agitation regarding alleged Anglo-American agreements with Thailand and Japanese military pressure on French Indo-China.
subfiles.from: Harry I. T. Creswell, Military Attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: The concluding portion (pages 6 and 7) of Military Attaché Report No. 10,242 analyzes Japanese press reactions to rumors of Anglo-American agreements with Thailand, noting that Japan sought to exploit Thai border claims against French Indo-China without encouraging foreign interference in Thailand. It also details increasing Japanese military pressure on local French authorities in Indo-China, specifically the prevention of foreign supplies from reaching Nationalist China. Creswell assesses that the Japanese are positioning themselves for further southward expansion toward Singapore.
subfiles.title: Military Attaché Report No. 10,242: Developments in Thailand and French Indo-China
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department

subfiles.about: Reports on a joint representation made by the Japanese Navy and War Ministers demanding Cabinet support for the Imperial Rule Assistance Association and war economy expansion.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that the Japanese Navy Minister, speaking also for the Minister of War at a Cabinet meeting, demanded the healthy development of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association, the strengthening of wartime economic productivity, and the elimination of rumors and political plots. Grew interprets this step as an effort by the military leadership to dispel rumors of disunity, reaffirm complete support for the Konoe Cabinet, and ensure that civil authorities and economic circles comply with government reform programs.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1248 from Tokyo regarding Military Demands on the Cabinet

subfiles.about: Calls attention to statements by the Japanese Cabinet Information Bureau concerning the elimination of capitalists and the creation of a totalitarian world order.
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Adviser on Political Relations, calls the attention of Under Secretary Sumner Welles to official Japanese statements in an attached naval intelligence report. Specifically, Hornbeck highlights declarations by the Cabinet Information Bureau asserting that Japan's domestic 'New Order' aims to secure a minimum standard of living, abolish capitalists, and position Japan as the locomotive force in establishing a totalitarian world to replace liberal ideas.
subfiles.title: Memorandum regarding Cabinet Information Bureau Statements on the 'New Order'

subfiles.about: Summarizes the findings of Naval Intelligence Report No. 181 on Japan's official explanations of its domestic and foreign policies.
subfiles.summary: Herbert M. Fales of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs provides a summary of ONI Report No. 181 dated October 31, 1940. The memorandum reviews the Cabinet Information Bureau's concepts of the Greater East Asia Sphere, the replacement of majority rule with government authoritarian decision-making, and the three guiding principles of national defense reform and spiritual cooperation under the Imperial wishes.
subfiles.title: Memorandum summarizing Naval Intelligence Report No. 181 on Japan's 'New Order'

subfiles.about: Details and analyzes official Japanese definitions of the 'New Order' in foreign policy and the totalitarian restructuring of Japanese domestic society.
subfiles.from: H. H. Smith-Hutton, Naval Attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Lieutenant Commander Smith-Hutton examines the phrase 'New Order,' concluding that in international affairs it denotes 'Asia for the Japanese,' while domestically it describes efforts to institute a Japanese-style totalitarian state. The report quotes extensively from official publications of the Cabinet Information Bureau and statements by Prince Konoe and Rear Admiral Gumpei Sekine regarding the abolition of political parties, austerity measures, social controls, and the structure of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association. It notes that the new system replaces liberal individualism with total state mobilization under the Emperor.
subfiles.title: ONI Intelligence Report No. 181: The New Order - Official Explanations of Japan's Domestic and Foreign Policies
subfiles.to: Director of Naval Intelligence, Navy Department

subfiles.about: Transmits and highlights key points of Consul Walter P. McConaughy's memorandum on political and economic trends in western Japan.
subfiles.summary: Frank A. Schuler, Jr. of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs submits to Assistant Secretary Grady an attached memorandum prepared by Consul Walter P. McConaughy, who had returned from Osaka for consultation. Schuler highlights McConaughy's analysis of why formerly moderate and liberal Japanese elements have come to endorse aggressive foreign policy, the restraining influence of Osaka commercial circles on radical military groups, and the prevailing sentiment in western Japan against economic reprisals against the United States.
subfiles.title: Memorandum regarding Consul McConaughy's Observations on Western Japan

subfiles.about: Analyzes the political and economic attitudes of business and moderate leaders in western Japan toward government policy and the United States.
subfiles.from: Walter P. McConaughy, Consul at Osaka
subfiles.summary: Consul McConaughy reports on observations made in the Osaka-Kobe region prior to his departure on September 14, 1940. He notes a disturbing trend among formerly moderate business and intellectual leaders toward uncritical endorsement of Japanese foreign policy and acceptance of police control and economic regimentation. However, he highlights that conservative industrial leaders, represented in the Cabinet by Communications Minister Murata and Commerce Minister Kobayashi, exercise a practical restraining influence against military radicalism, successfully preserving the cotton spinning export trade and opposing economic reprisals against the United States.
subfiles.title: Observations on the Japanese Political Situation as Noted in Western Japan

subfiles.about: Reports the appointment of Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma and Naoki Hoshino as Ministers-without-portfolio in the Konoe Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew informs the Department of State that evening newspapers announced the appointment of former Premier Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma and Cabinet Planning Board Director Naoki Hoshino as Ministers-without-portfolio. He notes that a special Imperial ordinance will be promulgated to permit the appointment of Ministers-without-portfolio from outside the ranks of career government officials.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1277 from Tokyo regarding Cabinet Appointments of Hiranuma and Hoshino

subfiles.about: Analyzes Japanese press reactions and the political strengthening of the Konoe Cabinet through the addition of Baron Hiranuma.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that the Japanese vernacular press unanimously regards the appointment of Baron Hiranuma as Minister-without-portfolio as a major strengthening of the Konoe Cabinet against rightist criticism and sabotage. Press commentary indicates that Hiranuma's presence will bolster the prestige of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association, quell rumors that the new structure is unconstitutional or communistic, and provide strong civilian leadership alongside Prince Konoe. Grew observes that, combined with the recent military demarche, this move indicates the government intends to maintain stability through the forthcoming Diet session without changing fundamental policies.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1279 from Tokyo analyzing the Political Significance of Hiranuma's Appointment

subfiles.about: Reports statements by Foreign Minister Matsuoka to foreign correspondents asserting that he and Prince Konoe represent a minority opposing Western ideas of conquest.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports on information received from an American correspondent regarding an interview given by Foreign Minister Yosuke Matsuoka to foreign journalists. Matsuoka asserted that he and Prince Konoe represent a minority in Japan struggling against a group enamored with Western ideas of conquest, oppression, and exploitation, and warned that if that group succeeded, Japan would be doomed to failure. Grew notes that while foreign correspondents cabled these statements abroad, the Japanese domestic press omitted all reference to these remarks.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1309 from Tokyo regarding Foreign Minister Matsuoka's Press Interview

subfiles.about: Transmits strictly confidential copies of correspondence and memoranda concerning M. Kleiman's proposal to send a special American emissary to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State transmits to Ambassador Grew in Tokyo, for his strictly confidential information, copies of an undated letter and 24-page memorandum received from New York businessman M. Kleiman, the Department's reply of December 5, 1940, and internal State Department memoranda of December 23 and December 30, 1940. The documents relate to Kleiman's recommendation that a special unofficial American emissary be dispatched to Tokyo to negotiate a reconciliation with moderate Japanese factions.
subfiles.title: Diplomatic Instruction to Tokyo regarding the Kleiman Proposal for a Special Emissary
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo

subfiles.about: Explains the diplomatic objections to M. Kleiman's proposal for sending a clandestine emissary to negotiate with Japanese political factions.
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck criticizes M. Kleiman's proposal that the United States send someone sub rosa to confer with political factions in Japan. Hornbeck asserts that the United States cannot properly negotiate with dissident factions within a foreign nation, arguing that if official spokesmen do not represent the true voice of a country, that nation must set up other spokesmen for itself. He also emphasizes that it would be utterly impossible to dispatch an emissary of the required caliber on a clandestine basis.
subfiles.title: Memorandum regarding the Inadvisability of Sending a Sub Rosa Emissary to Japan

subfiles.about: Summarizes and evaluates M. Kleiman's letter and 24-page memorandum regarding internal conditions in Japan and his proposal for a special reconciliation emissary.
subfiles.from: Colville, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Colville of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs analyzes materials submitted by New York businessman M. Kleiman following his return from Japan. The memorandum summarizes Kleiman's views on the historical consistency of U.S. Far Eastern policy, the internal economic and spiritual strain in Japan, the anti-capitalist radicalism of Colonel Kingoro Hashimoto's movement, and the demoralization leading to the Tripartite Pact. It also outlines Kleiman's discussions in Tokyo with prominent Japanese leaders such as former Finance Minister Sotaro Ishiwata, Count Yoriyasu Arima, Admiral Yonai, and General Araki, who allegedly favored sending a special unofficial American envoy to arrange a bilateral reconciliation.
subfiles.title: Memorandum analyzing M. Kleiman's Letter and Proposal for a Special Emissary to Japan

subfiles.about: Urges the State Department to dispatch an unofficial American emissary to Japan to negotiate a reconciliation with moderate Japanese leaders.
subfiles.summary: Businessman M. Kleiman writes to Maxwell M. Hamilton detailing his observations of internal demoralization, economic distress, and plummeting stock values in Japan following adherence to the Axis alliance. He asserts that traditional Japanese vested interests—capital, the army, and the navy—fear the radical socialist and anti-capitalist threat represented by Colonel Hashimoto and desperately desire a rapprochement with the United States. Kleiman recounts personal conversations with influential figures including Admiral Yonai, former Premier Okada, former Finance Minister Ishiwata, Count Arima, and younger military officers, claiming they support reconciliation and offering to arrange an official invitation for an American emissary through Count Arima.
subfiles.title: Letter from M. Kleiman to Maxwell M. Hamilton advocating a Special Emissary to Japan

subfiles.about: Comprehensive 24-page analysis of the historical evolution of U.S. Far Eastern policy, Japanese cabinet politics, economic dislocation, and the circumstances surrounding Japan's entry into the Axis.
subfiles.summary: Kleiman provides an extensive analysis tracing U.S. Far Eastern policy since the 1899 Open Door notes and contrasts its constancy with the confusing and contradictory course of Japanese diplomacy. He examines the domestic consequences of the China war boom, severe inflation, the National Spiritual Mobilization campaign, and the disruptive anti-luxury regulations that paralyzed commerce. The memorandum chronicles the collapse of political parties from the 1937 Konoe cabinet through the Yonai administration, the rise of the New Structure and the Imperial Rule Assistance Association, and the extremist anti-capitalist influence of Colonel Kingoro Hashimoto. Finally, Kleiman examines the diplomatic intrigue led by Toshio Shiratori and Heinrich Stahmer that culminated in the Tripartite Pact, arguing that adherence to the Axis alienated the United States without solving any of Japan's fundamental economic or military problems.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by M. Kleiman on United States-Japanese Relations and Internal Conditions in Japan

subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of M. Kleiman's letter and memorandum regarding political developments in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Chief of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, sends a formal acknowledgment to M. Kleiman for his undated letter and enclosed memorandum delivered on December 2, 1940. Hamilton states that the contents of the letter and accompanying analysis have been noted with care and expresses appreciation for Kleiman's courtesy in bringing his views to the attention of the Department of State.
subfiles.title: Letter from Maxwell M. Hamilton acknowledging M. Kleiman's Submission

subfiles.about: Reports that foreign and Chinese newspapers in Shanghai published Foreign Minister Matsuoka's interview remarks while Japanese-controlled media suppressed them.
subfiles.summary: Consul General Lockhart reports from Shanghai with reference to Tokyo's telegram No. 1309 concerning Foreign Minister Matsuoka's interview with foreign correspondents. He confirms that local American, British, and pro-Chungking Chinese newspapers carried full reports of Matsuoka's remarks regarding his struggle against Japanese elements favoring Western methods of conquest. In contrast, Japanese-language newspapers and Japanese-controlled Chinese dailies published the official Domei news agency version, which omitted those specific statements.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1379 from Shanghai regarding Foreign Press Coverage of Matsuoka's Interview

subfiles.about: Summarizes Ambassador Grew's despatch concerning the political maneuvers to manage the Japanese Diet under the 'New Structure.'
subfiles.summary: Herbert M. Fales of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs summarizes Ambassador Grew's Despatch No. 5154 of November 20, 1940. The memorandum outlines efforts by leaders of the 'New Structure' to preserve the outward appearance of parliamentary government during the Diet session convening on December 24, 1940, while preventing the legislature from voicing opposition. It highlights the establishment of a 100-member 'Diet Bureau' within the Imperial Rule Assistance Association designed to steer parliamentary deliberations and secure the substance of totalitarianism without violating constitutional forms.
subfiles.title: Memorandum summarizing Tokyo Despatch No. 5154 on the Japanese Diet and the 'New Structure'

subfiles.about: Analyzes the projected role of the Imperial Diet under the 'New Structure' and efforts to ensure parliamentary compliance.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew provides an in-depth analysis of the forthcoming convocation of the Imperial Diet on December 24, 1940, viewing it as a critical test of national solidarity under Prince Konoe's 'New Structure.' He traces the decade-long decline of political party influence culminating in voluntary party dissolution in the House of Representatives, while contrasting this with the stubborn refusal of aristocratic factions in the House of Peers to dissolve. Grew details the organizational mechanisms devised to control the Diet, notably the creation of a Diet Bureau within the Imperial Rule Assistance Association, and concludes that while Konoe seeks to respect constitutional formalities to avoid public shock, Japan is moving toward the substance of an authoritarian, totalitarian state.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 5154: The Position of the Japanese Diet in Relation to the 'New Structure'

subfiles.about: Duplicate carbon copy of the first four pages of Ambassador Grew's Despatch No. 5154 on the Japanese Diet and the 'New Structure.'
subfiles.summary: This subfile consists of a duplicate carbon copy of pages 1 through 4 of Ambassador Joseph C. Grew's Despatch No. 5154 dated November 20, 1940. It reproduces Grew's reporting on the convocation of the Diet, the decline of parliamentary government since the Inukai Cabinet, historical interpellations by Takao Saito, the resistance to dissolution within the House of Peers, and the initial setup of the Diet Bureau within the Imperial Rule Assistance Association.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 5154: The Position of the Japanese Diet in Relation to the 'New Structure' (Duplicate Copy)
